idiom_name: class instance identity with === and ObjectIdentifier
implementation_notes: Because classes are reference types, an entity modelled as a class already has identity: === and !== test whether two references denote the same instance, and ObjectIdentifier(instance) yields a stable (process-lifetime) identity usable as a dictionary key. The pattern's remaining work is the durable identity - store a let id (a UUID or typed identity) on the class so the entity is recognisable after being persisted and reloaded, and keep attribute changes behind methods - and note that == is something you define yourself: conforming a class to Equatable by id is a deliberate choice. The standard library's Identifiable provides ObjectIdentifier as the default id for class types, which is only unique for the lifetime of the object, so replace it with the persisted id.
pitfalls: == on two references with the same id is false unless Equatable is implemented; relying on == without implementing it compares instance identity, not entity identity.

Modelling the entity as a struct - the default choice in Swift - gives value semantics and no identity at all: two copies are independent, === does not compile, and synthesized Equatable compares attributes.
Identifiable's default id for class types is ObjectIdentifier, which changes on every launch and after re-creation; supply the persisted id or the same customer is not recognised after reload.

variants.name: Entity as an Identifiable value type with a stable id
variants.idiom_name: struct conforming to Identifiable with a persisted id (diffing-friendly)
variants.implementation_notes: When the entity is handled as a value - SwiftUI state, snapshots, collections that are diffed - the Swift idiom is a struct conforming to Identifiable whose id is the stable business or persisted identifier; Equatable/Hashable can then be implemented from the id alone so copies of the same entity compare equal, and updates replace the whole value instead of mutating shared state. This trades reference identity for consistency: no ===, no aliasing, and the identity must be carried by the id through every copy, which is exactly what the standard-library protocol exists for (distinguishing an entity's identity from the snapshot of its state). Mixing the two styles for one concept - a class entity plus struct snapshots - is the usual source of bugs.
pitfalls: Synthesized Equatable/Hashable compares all stored properties, so two snapshots of the same entity with different state are unequal; implement equality from the id when identity semantics are wanted.
The id must be the durable identifier, not UUID() generated per initializer call, or every copy and every reload looks like a new entity to diffing algorithms.
A struct entity has no shared identity: two copies can diverge silently and mutations must be written back explicitly to the store.
